hookLine: the Chmielnicki uprising destroys Jewish communities in Ukraine
carry: a number that stands for real people

lines: A NUMBER THAT IS A MEMORY.
cards: Jewish memory has its own way of naming years. In the Hebrew calendar, years are written with letters, and two short letter-words, tach and tat, came to stand for a time of terror in Poland and Ukraine.
Jews spoke of the decrees of tach and tat the way other people say a date they cannot forget. In the ordinary calendar, the first of those years is a single number, and it is today's title.

teach.b: In the lands of Ukraine then ruled by Poland, the Cossacks rose up under a leader named Bohdan Chmielnicki.
The uprising had its own grievances, against Polish lords and their power over the land and the people who worked it.
Jews were caught in the middle. Some served the lords as stewards and leaseholders, collecting rents and running mills and inns, so in the rebels' eyes they stood for the lords.

As the rebels moved through the towns, Jewish communities were attacked and destroyed. People fled to fortified towns, and some of those towns fell. Families were killed, taken captive, or forced to convert.
The chronicles give large numbers, and historians still argue over them. What no one disputes is that whole communities disappeared.
A survivor named Nathan Hannover wrote a chronicle of those years, in plain Hebrew, town by town, so people would know.

teach.h: DEEP MIRE, WHERE THERE IS NO STANDING.
teach.b: He took its title from a drowning cry in the Psalms: "I am sunk in deep mire, where there is no standing." Deep mire, in Hebrew, is yeven metzulah.
Afterward, the rabbis of Poland set aside a day of fasting and lament, and some communities kept it long afterward. A massacre in these lessons is not a plot twist.
It is a number that stands for real people, names mostly lost, held in a people's memory.

how: Jews remember the massacres of 1648 in chronicles, memorial prayers and laments, and some communities long kept a fast day for them.

games.q: you survived the destruction of your town. what do you do with what you saw?
o: write it down, town by town, so people know.
turn it into a legend with a happy ending.
games.why: Nathan Hannover wrote a chronicle in plain Hebrew and named it deep mire, from the Psalms.

practice: Sit still and let your hands rest open; there's no need to picture anything violent.
Just hold in mind that there were towns, and in them families, someone baking bread, a child learning letters, an old man at prayer, and let the silence be for them.
If you pray, you can remember them in your own words, or with no words at all.
